chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Sa'd ibn Isma'il from his father Isma'il ibn Isa who said:

I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered animals of the Jews and Christians and their food, and he said: Yes. First, among these narrations is that they do not contradict the earlier narrations because the earlier ones are more numerous. Also, among those who narrated these narrations is one who narrated what we mentioned earlier regarding the prohibition of their milk, namely Abu Basir and Muhammad ibn Muslim. And if it were safe from all of this afterwards, it would still carry two possibilities: one of which is that we apply it to the state of necessity, not the state of choice, because at the time of necessity the dead animal becomes permissible, so how much more so the slaughtered animal of one who differs from Islam, and that which indicates this.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating the meat of Jews and Christians according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents this narration from Imam al-Rida to address the apparent tension between the permissibility of Jewish and Christian meat and the prohibition of their milk, noting that the former is supported by numerous chains of transmission. He offers a nuanced juristic resolution: even if not contradictory, the permissibility of their meat is primarily understood as applying to a state of necessity (darurah) rather than voluntary choice, drawing an analogy to the permissibility of carrion in times of need. This reflects the Shia scholarly approach of harmonizing conflicting reports through contextual interpretation and hierarchical evidence.
